## Proof

We determine the values of $p$ for which

$$
S \;=\; \sum_{n=N}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\,n\,(\log n)\,(\log\log n)\,\dotsm\,(\log_j n)\,(\log_{j+1} n)^{p}\,}
$$

converges, where $\log_0 n = n$, $\log_1 n = \log n$, $\log_2 n = \log\log n$, …, $\log_{j+1} n = \log(\log_j n)$, and $N$ is large enough that every iterated logarithm appearing is positive (so the terms are well defined and positive).

---

### Step 1. Reduction to an integral via the integral test

The summand $f(n) = \dfrac{1}{n(\log n)(\log\log n)\dotsm(\log_j n)(\log_{j+1} n)^p}$ is positive and (eventually) decreasing, since each factor in the denominator is positive and increasing for $n$ beyond the threshold where all iterated logarithms are defined. Hence the **integral test** applies:

$$
S \text{ converges} \iff \int_{N}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{\,x\,(\log x)\,(\log\log x)\,\dotsm\,(\log_j x)\,(\log_{j+1} x)^{p}\,} \text{ converges}.
$$

---

### Step 2. A telescoping substitution

Consider the indefinite integral

$$
I \;=\; \int \frac{dx}{\,x\,(\log x)\,(\log\log x)\,\dotsm\,(\log_j x)\,(\log_{j+1} x)^{p}\,}.
$$

We apply the chain of substitutions $u = \log_{j+1} x$. Recall that

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(\log_{j+1} x\bigr) \;=\; \frac{1}{x\,(\log x)\,(\log\log x)\,\dotsm\,(\log_j x)},
$$

because each differentiation of an iterated logarithm contributes exactly one factor $1/(\text{previous iterated logarithm})$ via the chain rule:

$$
(\log_{j+1} x)' = \frac{1}{\log_j x}\cdot(\log_j x)' = \frac{1}{\log_j x}\cdot\frac{1}{\log_{j-1} x}\cdot(\log_{j-1} x)' = \dots = \frac{1}{x(\log x)(\log\log x)\dotsm(\log_j x)}.
$$

Therefore the entire product $x(\log x)(\log\log x)\dotsm(\log_j x)$ in the denominator is precisely $\dfrac{dx}{d(\log_{j+1} x)}$, i.e.

$$
\frac{dx}{\,x\,(\log x)\,\dotsm\,(\log_j x)\,} \;=\; d\bigl(\log_{j+1} x\bigr).
$$

Substituting $u = \log_{j+1} x$:

$$
I \;=\; \int \frac{d(\log_{j+1} x)}{(\log_{j+1} x)^{p}} \;=\; \int \frac{du}{u^{p}} \;=\; \begin{cases} \dfrac{u^{1-p}}{1-p} + C, & p \neq 1,\\[6pt] \log u + C, & p = 1. \end{cases}
$$

---

### Step 3. Behavior at infinity

As $x \to \infty$, each iterated logarithm $\log_k x \to \infty$, so in particular $u = \log_{j+1} x \to \infty$.

**Case $p > 1$.** Then $1 - p < 0$, so $u^{1-p} \to 0$ as $u \to \infty$. The antiderivative $\dfrac{u^{1-p}}{1-p}$ has a finite limit at infinity, hence the improper integral converges, and therefore $S$ converges.

**Case $p = 1$.** The antiderivative is $\log u = \log(\log_{j+1} x) \to \infty$, so the integral diverges, and $S$ diverges.

**Case $p < 1$.** Then $1 - p > 0$, so $u^{1-p} \to \infty$, the integral diverges, and $S$ diverges.

---

### Step 4. Conclusion

The series converges if and only if $p > 1$.

$$
\boxed{\,p > 1\,}
$$
